chunks: Al-Hasan ibn Mahbub from a man who said: Abd Allah ibn Sulayman told me: I heard Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

A woman asked him, saying: 'My daughter died and there was no impediment preventing her from performing Hajj, so should I perform Hajj on her behalf?' He said, 'Yes.' She said: 'She was a slave-girl.' He said: 'There is no harm for you in making supplication, for it enters upon her just as a gift enters the house.'
ai.seo_question: What is the ruling on performing Hajj for a deceased daughter who was a slave-girl, and is supplication sufficient?
ai.summary: In this narration from *Tahdhib al-Ahkam*, Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) clarifies the ruling for a deceased slave-girl who was capable of Hajj but did not perform it; while a free person's Hajj is obligatory to be performed by another, the Imam advises that supplication (*dua*) suffices for the slave, likening its spiritual benefit to a gift entering a home. This highlights the Shia scholarly distinction between the legal obligations of free and slave individuals in ritual worship, emphasizing the enduring efficacy of intercessory prayer for the deceased.
